Dagger network metrics

From useful estimates to exact totals

How we measure network traffic without confusing container-to-container transfers with traffic that leaves Dagger.

RX
TX network layer

01 · The goal

Answer two different questions

How much left Dagger?

A complete network-layer total, split between internal and external endpoints.

Which operation caused it?

A useful estimate attached to withExec, HTTP, Git, registry, filesync, sockets, tunnels, and LLM operations.

One counter cannot answer both questions well.
Coverage and attribution are separate problems
02 · The original problem

One number merged two very different transfers

32
MiB from another Dagger container
+
8
MiB from the Internet
=
40
MiB reported as “Network Tx”

The old host-veth counter mixed internal and external bytes. Its direction was also reversed: host-side TX is container-side RX.

Correct bytes, wrong meaning
03 · A larger blind spot

Not every transfer happens inside a user container

User request
→
Dagger engine
→
HTTP · Git · Registry
Filesync · LLM
→
Remote endpoint

Container traffic

  • Visible on the container veth
  • Includes withExec and services

Engine traffic

  • Can bypass every user-container veth
  • Still needs complete accounting
A veth-only solution cannot cover the engine
04 · First attempt

Measure where each operation reads or writes data

HTTP

Count response-body bytes.

Git

Parse the received pack size from progress.

Registry

Count manifests, config, and compressed layers.

Filesync

Count bytes at copy boundaries.

Sockets & tunnels

Count payload copied in each direction.

LLM

Count request and response bodies.

Excellent attribution. Incomplete network totals.
These became the per-operation estimates
05 · Limits of application measurement

The payload is not the packet

What we can assign

  • HTTP body bytes
  • Git compressed pack size
  • Registry layer payloads
  • Bytes copied for one operation

What may be shared or missing

  • IP, TCP, TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 overhead
  • Connection setup and retransmissions
  • One connection multiplexed across operations
  • Long-lived pooled connections

Per-operation values are deliberately labeled estimates. Pretending otherwise would create false precision.

Useful for attribution, not authoritative totals
06 · Final design

A hybrid model

Authoritative total

eBPF

Counts traffic at the engine cgroup boundary. Complete across the engine and its child cgroups.

Per-operation attribution

APP

Measures payload at each operation’s transfer boundary. Useful, but approximate.

Exact total answers “how much?” · Estimates answer “which operation?”
Two views, one coherent model
07 · Classification

Realm and destination are independent

Internal endpoint
External endpoint
Userland
Userland · internal

A user container downloads from another Dagger service.

Userland · external

User work reaches GitHub, a registry, or an Internet API.

Daggerland
Daggerland · internal

The engine talks to an official SDK runtime on a Dagger network.

Daggerland · external

The engine downloads a trusted runtime or helper image.

External userland is the chargeable class in the proposed model—typically TX for provider egress.

Who caused it? · Where did it go?
08 · Exact totals

Count every network packet

Dagger watches network traffic from the engine and every container it starts.

1 · See itA packet is sent or received.
→
2 · Measure itCount the whole IP packet, including headers.
→
3 · Label itRecord who owns it, where it went, and its direction.
User code sends a 1,500-byte packet to the Internet userland · external · TX · 1,500 bytes
The result is one exact, engine-wide total
09 · Exact totals in code

This is the exact counter

SEC("cgroup_skb/egress") int count_cgroup_egress(struct __sk_buff *skb) { return add_owner_bytes(skb, DIR_TX); } __u8 scope = classify_l3(skb, direction); __u8 owner = packet_owner(skb, direction); ... *bytes += skb->len;
  • egress: run for every outgoing packet
  • DIR_TX: record it as transmitted
  • scope: internal or external destination
  • owner: userland or daggerland
  • skb->len: add the full IP packet size
engine/ebpf/nettracer/bpf/netbytes.bpf.c · add_owner_bytes + count_cgroup_egress
10 · Realm in code

Assign the realm before traffic starts

Engine sockets use a realm-specific dialer. Child processes inherit the realm of their cgroup.

A userland TCP connection

dialer := realm.Userland.Dialer(net.Dialer{}) conn, err := dialer.DialContext( ctx, "tcp", address, )

A daggerland HTTP pool

client := realm.Daggerland.HTTPClient( baseTransport, ) resp, err := client.Do(req)

A fixed pool has one immutable realm. For request-selected pools, realm.With marks the context and realm.NewTransport chooses a separate userland or daggerland pool.

No realm means no new engine connection in strict mode
11 · Telemetry outputs

Two metric families, clearly labeled

Per-operation estimates

dagger.io/metrics.network.rx.bytes dagger.io/metrics.network.tx.bytes withExec · http · git container.from · registry.push filesync · host.socket · host.tunnel · llm

Authoritative totals

dagger_network_bytes_total dagger_network_accounting_available dagger_network_unattributed_bytes_total dagger_network_unattributed_packets_total dagger_network_realm_enforced
Legacy netstat metrics are removed
12 · Reconciliation

The difference is visible, not invented

authoritative external userland total
− sum of matching operation estimates
= unallocated protocol + shared-connection bytes

What we can do

Show the residual explicitly, compare it over time, and allocate it proportionally in a report if desired.

What we should not do

Claim that shared TLS or HTTP/2 connection overhead belongs exactly to one operation.

The exact total stays exact. The operation breakdown stays honest about uncertainty.

No bytes disappear; some bytes remain unattributed to one operation
13 · Live demo

What to point out

1 · Old view

40 MiB merges a 32 MiB internal download and an 8 MiB external download.

2 · New exec view

32 MiB internal and 8 MiB external appear separately, in container direction.

3 · Engine totals

HTTP, Git, image, registry, filesync, socket, tunnel, and exec traffic all appear in cgroup totals.

dagger shell -W github.com/dagger/dagger@pull/14159/head \ engine-dev:playground ./hack/demo-network-metrics.sh

The demo also checks strict realms, successful cgroup registration, and the absence of legacy netstat metrics.
